title: AI edge steps up cyber threat to power grid
full_text:
Frontier artificial intelligence models weaponised by bad actors have emerged as a major risk to Australia’s energy grid, with the threat of cyber attacks expected to escalate monthsrather than years, the Australian Energy Market Operator has warned.
The power grid operator said there had been a “paradigm shift” in the capability of cyber threats with AI models tapping advanced skills in reading, reasoning and manipulating code, allowing greater automation across the cyber threat chain.
AI advancements had lowered the bar for “specialised expertise previously required to target critical infrastructure”, increasing risk across the power system, including energy plants. “Assessments of recently developed AI systems have demonstrated the potential to support multi-step cyber attacks involving industrial and operational technology environ-ments,” AEMO said in a report on grid security.
Anthropic said last week that software it was testing accessed the internet and hacked companies in three separate incidents dating back to April. OpenAI also revealed its model had broken out of a testing sandbox – a digital prison supposed to be disconnected from the internet – and hacked the an AI company.
AEMO said advice from the Five Eyes cyber security agencies had underscored that frontier AI models were rapidly changing the cyber threat environment.
“Lower barriers to entry mean that poorly secured or legacy systems may become more attractive targets for increasingly capable threat actors,” AEMO said. “For the national electricity market, the implications extend beyond individual organisations, as cyber vulnerabilities affecting key market participants, suppliers or operational service providers could impact operational continuity and market confidence.” In early 2025, The Australian reported AEMO will take a central role in the event of a cyber attack against infrastructure.
Australia has the world’s largest per-household rooftop solar-powered electricity generation.
But the increased number of solar panels has created a security flaw, as the bulk of solar inverters are made in China and connected to the internet. In July, the Australian Signals Directorate issued a joint statement with authorities from a dozen other nations warning hackers from the Russian Federal Security Service Centre 16 continue to manipulate compromised critical infrastructure networks. The industries most at risk include energy, communications, defence, health, finance and government services.
